articles.title: Einstein's equations may explain the universe without dark energy
articles.summary: Mathematicians have uncovered what they argue is a fundamental flaw in the standard model of the universe, potentially challenging the need for dark energy. Their calculations suggest that the mathematical framework used to describe cosmic expansion is inherently unstable and that the universe could accelerate naturally under Einstein's original theory of gravity. The findings also raise surprising questions about whether our location in the universe is as ordinary as scientists have long assumed.
articles.content:
Mathematicians are raising a major challenge to one of modern cosmology's most widely accepted explanations: the idea that dark energy is driving the accelerating expansion of the universe.

A study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society A presents mathematical findings that researchers at the University of California, Davis, say reveal a fundamental instability in the standard model of the expanding universe. Their calculations suggest that cosmic acceleration could emerge naturally from Einstein's equations, potentially eliminating the need to invoke mysterious dark energy.

The work challenges the Lambda-cold dark matter model, the leading framework scientists use to describe the universe's evolution since the Big Bang. The researchers reached their conclusions by studying the Einstein-Euler equations, which combine Einstein's theory of general relativity with equations describing how fluids behave. Together, these mathematical tools help scientists investigate everything from galaxies and black holes to the expansion of the cosmos.

A Hidden Instability in Our Model of the Universe

To explain the problem, Blake Temple, the study's corresponding author and a distinguished professor emeritus of mathematics at UC Davis, offered a simple comparison: a pencil balanced vertically on its tip.

"All the forces are in balance when a pencil is standing on end, so it is a 'solution of the equations,'" he said. "But it's unstable. Any breath of air and it falls away."

According to Temple, the team's mathematical analysis shows that Friedmann spacetimes, which form the foundation of conventional models of cosmic expansion, are unstable at both small and large scales in the context of the Big Bang. He described the standard solution as exceptionally unstable.

"Unstable solutions in physics and science are considered not physical," Temple said. "You'll never observe them in nature."

This instability could have far-reaching consequences. If the universe naturally evolves away from the behavior predicted by these conventional models, its accelerating expansion might not require a separate form of energy to explain it. Instead, Temple argues, the answer could already be contained within Einstein's original theory of gravity.

"The instability of all Friedmann spacetimes to accelerated expansion suggests a simpler, more natural explanation for the acceleration of the universe than dark energy," he said.

Why Scientists Believe Dark Energy Is Expanding the Universe

For nearly three decades, dark energy has been the leading explanation for one of astronomy's most puzzling discoveries: the universe is not simply expanding, but its expansion is accelerating.

The concept has roots in Einstein's groundbreaking 1915 theory of general relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of space and time. Einstein originally believed the universe was static, neither expanding nor contracting. To make his equations compatible with that assumption, he introduced a mathematical term that counteracted gravity, calling it the "cosmological constant."

That assumption changed after Edwin Hubble discovered evidence in 1929 that the universe was expanding. Einstein famously referred to his introduction of the cosmological constant as his "biggest blunder," since his original equations without the additional term could have predicted an expanding universe.

The cosmological constant returned to prominence in the 1990s, when astronomers discovered that cosmic expansion was speeding up. It became closely associated with dark energy, the name given to the unknown component thought to be responsible for this acceleration.

Today's standard cosmological framework builds on the Friedmann universe, a mathematical description in which space expands while matter remains evenly distributed across the cosmos at any given moment. This assumption of large-scale uniformity plays a central role in how scientists reconstruct the universe's history.

But Temple and his collaborators began questioning whether the underlying mathematics could remain stable, prompting them to investigate other possible explanations for the observed acceleration.

Could Einstein's Equations Explain Cosmic Acceleration?

The researchers initially considered whether a massive shockwave might help explain the universe's expansion and the unexpected acceleration associated with it.

"Our first idea was that maybe the universe was expanding because there was a shockwave, and the anomalous acceleration was the expanding wave behind that shockwave," Temple said. "Then we realized there's a family of self-similar solutions during the radiation epoch of the Big Bang, which might model that expanding wave."

In mathematics and physics, self-similar solutions describe patterns that retain their underlying structure when viewed at different scales. A familiar example is a fractal, in which similar shapes can appear at increasingly larger or smaller sizes.

The researchers identified a family of these solutions associated with the radiation-dominated period of the early universe, when radiation played a major role in determining how the cosmos evolved.

Building on their earlier work, they used a self-similar form of Einstein's equations to represent the standard cosmological model as a rest point, a mathematical state in which the system's defining variables remain unchanged. This approach allowed them to examine whether small departures from that state would disappear or grow over time.

Their analysis provided a mathematical framework for evaluating the stability of the standard model and, more broadly, Friedmann spacetimes during the matter-dominated era of the early universe, when matter became more influential than radiation.

A Mathematical Challenge to the Standard Big Bang Model

The results suggest that the conventional mathematical descriptions of the expanding universe are vulnerable to disturbances that grow rather than fade.

"We prove that, like Einstein's static model, the Friedmann spacetimes are all unstable to radial perturbation at large length scales," Temple said. "This appears to rule out the Lambda-cold dark matter model as a viable stable solution of the Einstein equations of general relativity, with or without dark energy."

Radial perturbations are disturbances that change with distance from a central point. In the researchers' mathematical framework, such changes can cause the behavior of an expanding universe to depart from the predictions of the standard Friedmann model.

"This means," he added, "that the Big Bang should generically look exactly like a Friedmann spacetime near the center of symmetry, but generically one should observe accelerations away from Friedmann far from the center."

In other words, the universe could behave much like the standard model predicts near a central region while exhibiting different expansion behavior farther away.

The researchers argue that this instability may offer a natural route to accelerated cosmic expansion without adding a cosmological constant or invoking dark energy. Their calculations indicate that the acceleration can emerge directly from the Einstein-Euler equations themselves.

The findings represent a theoretical challenge to standard cosmology rather than observational proof that dark energy is unnecessary. Establishing whether this alternative can describe the actual universe would require determining how well its predictions match astronomical observations.

Does the Universe Have a Special Location?

Beyond the dark energy question, the study also raises a more fundamental issue involving the Copernican principle.

Named after astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, who helped overturn the belief that Earth sits at the center of the solar system, the principle holds that our location in the universe is not fundamentally special or privileged.

This assumption has become an important part of modern cosmology, supporting the view that the universe looks broadly similar when observed from different locations on sufficiently large scales.

The researchers' alternative mathematical framework introduces a center of spherical symmetry, raising questions about where an observer would need to be located for the model to agree with observations.

Temple argues that the Copernican principle must be applied consistently when evaluating competing explanations of the universe.

"Both the Lambda-cold dark matter model and a spherically symmetric spacetime produce a special place where we must lie for the model to be physically plausible," Temple said. "If this principle rules out one, it has to rule out the other."

The work opens another avenue for investigating why the universe's expansion is accelerating. Although dark energy remains a central component of the prevailing cosmological model, the researchers contend that the mathematics of general relativity may offer a different explanation for the same phenomenon.

If further theoretical and observational work supports their interpretation, it could lead to a significant reassessment of how scientists understand cosmic expansion and the mathematical foundations of the Big Bang.

The research received funding from the United Kingdom's Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council and the American Institute of Mathematics SQuaREs Program.

articles.personality_title: Mathematicians find new explanation for universe’s accelerating expansion
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For decades, scientists have believed that a mysterious force called dark energy is causing the universe to expand faster and faster. This idea is based on the standard model of cosmology, which uses Einstein’s theory of gravity combined with other assumptions about how the universe behaves.

**What happened** – A team of mathematicians at the University of California, Davis, studied the equations that describe the universe’s expansion. They discovered that the usual mathematical model is unstable, meaning it can change unexpectedly. Their work suggests that the universe’s acceleration might happen naturally through Einstein’s original gravity equations without needing dark energy.

**Impact** – This discovery challenges the main explanation for cosmic acceleration and offers a simpler idea based on existing physics. It also questions whether our place in the universe is ordinary, as the new model introduces a center point that might be special. This could change how scientists think about the universe’s growth and its overall structure.

**What’s next step** – Researchers will need to compare their new model’s predictions with real observations of the universe to see if it matches what telescopes and satellites detect. If it does, it might lead to revising the current cosmic model and how we understand space and time.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New mathematical findings suggest the universe’s accelerating expansion might come directly from Einstein’s gravity without dark energy, opening fresh questions about cosmic structure.

articles.personality_title_es: Matemáticos encuentran nueva explicación para la expansión acelerada del universo
articles.personality_presentation_es:

También plantea preguntas sobre si nuestra ubicación en el universo es común, ya que el nuevo modelo introduce un punto central que podría ser especial. Esto podría cambiar la forma en que los científicos entienden el crecimiento y la estructura general del universo.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores deberán comparar las predicciones de su nuevo modelo con las observaciones reales del universo para ver si coinciden con lo que detectan telescopios y satélites. Si es así, podría llevar a revisar el modelo cósmico actual y nuestra comprensión del espacio y el tiempo.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Nuevos hallazgos matemáticos sugieren que la expansión acelerada del universo podría surgir directamente de la gravedad de Einstein sin energía oscura, abriendo nuevas preguntas sobre la estructura cósmica.

articles.title: NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found
articles.summary: When a rose-colored meteorite was found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, no one knew how old it was or where it came from. Not until NASA-funded scientists age-dated its minerals did they realize the nearly 2-pound (800-gram) rock was a piece of Mars that formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one […]
articles.content:
Called Teghaza 001, this rose-colored rock is one of the most ancient Martian meteorites ever found on Earth. Credit: © Darryl Pitt / Maine Mineral & Gem Museum

When a rose-colored meteorite was found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, no one knew how old it was or where it came from. Not until NASA-funded scientists age-dated its minerals did they realize the nearly 2-pound (800-gram) rock was a piece of Mars that formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one of the oldest Martian meteorites ever found. Named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered, the meteorite is one of roughly 435 from the Red Planet.

In a paper published Thursday in Science, researchers offered an initial characterization of Teghaza 001, providing a rare snapshot of Mars’ ancient crust and formation. What scientists learn from future studies could help answer many questions, including how water and rocks interacted on ancient Mars. A separate paper published in Science Advances in June detailed the meteorite’s water content, offering a look at how water shaped the early planet’s surface.

“It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique,” said the paper’s lead author, Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars.”

This slice of Teghaza 001, a Martian meteorite, was used to study its mineralogy and chemistry. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

Rose-colored stone

What sets Teghaza 001 apart from other Martian meteorites is its texture and age as well as the uniqueness of its igneous, or volcanic, minerals. It is one of the three most ancient Martian meteorites found on Earth. While invaluable, the others provide more limited glimpses of Mars’ geological history. They include ALH84001, which is composed almost entirely of one mineral and is similar in age to Teghaza 001. The other meteorite, nicknamed “Black Beauty,” formed about 2.1 billion years ago and is composed of small, volcanic rock fragments.

Unlike its ancient peers, Teghaza 001 has a mix of igneous minerals that tells a story about how the planet’s crust formed from cooling magma before it was eventually altered by subsurface water. The meteorite’s distinctive mineralogy matches what NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter has observed in the planet’s cratered southern highlands. No one will ever know exactly where the meteorite originated on Mars, but the paper identifies several potential locations that match Teghaza 001’s mineralogy and chemistry.

“This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before,” said the new paper’s second author, Lee Saper, who conducted the research while at JPL as a postdoctoral scholar. Lee now is a scientist at NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley. “It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water.”

Although the Mars meteorites found on Earth differ from one another, they share a common history, having been blasted off the Red Planet’s surface by an impact, followed by a trajectory that eventually placed them on Earth and into the hands of scientists. Meteorites are often found by collectors in deserts or snowy plains, where they stand out from the rest of the barren landscape. Scientists can verify a meteorite as Martian by matching its mineral and chemical components to data collected by NASA’s Mars missions, including the Viking landers as well as the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers.

Scientists identified 13 locations on Mars that match the mineralogy and chemistry of Teghaza 001, one of the most ancient Martian meteorites ever found on Earth. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/USGS

Signs of water

When Liu was first asked to look at Teghaza 001, she almost passed on the opportunity.

Researchers at the University of New Mexico had already identified it as Martian based on its oxygen isotopes, which serve as geochemical fingerprints for different planetary bodies. In this case, the researchers matched the meteorite’s oxygen isotopes to those seen in other Martian meteorites. Teghaza 001 appeared to be a shergottite which is the most common class of meteorite from the Red Planet. As an expert in planetary samples, Liu has seen plenty of those, but she decided to take a peek, anyway.

At the very least, there were odd textures and unusual minerals she hadn’t seen before. Liu and her colleagues discovered zircon crystals in Teghaza 001, which record clues to a rock’s formation and can be used by geologists to precisely age-date a sample. Further analysis revealed when Teghaza 001 formed and when certain changes, like water alteration, occurred.

Caltech coauthor Francois Tissot helped the researchers utilize a novel age-dating method pioneered by his team. Compared with bulk-analysis techniques, where a sample is entirely dissolved and analyzed, Tissot’s in-situ rubidium-strontium age-dating used a piece of Teghaza 001 that was smaller than a fingernail, analyzing single mineral grains on its surface. Besides its extreme precision and speed, the technique preserves rare samples like Martian meteorites for future studies.

“Right now, we are one of very few labs in the world able to perform this kind of age-dating, and the first to date such an ancient Martian meteorite,” Tissot said. “Our hope is to pave the way for dating even more Martian meteorites, or samples returned from other planets, their moons, and asteroids.”

When the age-dating results came back, Liu was shocked: This rock had been altered by Martian water sometime around 4.1 billion years ago, suggesting it originally formed even earlier. Clues within the oxygen isotopes, texture, and chemistry of Teghaza 001 minerals point to a much more dynamic water cycle on early Mars.

This year’s papers are just the start. Liu and her co-authors are eager to see what the rest of the scientific community can learn from Teghaza 001.

“We’ve only scratched the surface,” Liu said.

-end-

articles.personality_title_es: Científicos datan una de las meteoritas marcianas más antiguas jamás encontradas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En 2022, se encontró una roca de color rosa en el desierto del Sahara. Los científicos no sabían de dónde venía ni qué edad tenía hasta que investigadores financiados por la NASA la estudiaron cuidadosamente.

**Qué pasó** – La roca, llamada Teghaza 001 por la llanura salada cercana en Malí, fue identificada como un fragmento de Marte formado hace más de 4.1 mil millones de años. Esto la convierte en una de las meteoritas marcianas más antiguas encontradas en la Tierra. Usando un nuevo método, los científicos dataron con precisión pequeños minerales dentro de la meteorita para conocer su edad e historia.

**Impacto** – Teghaza 001 es única porque tiene una mezcla de minerales volcánicos que cuentan cómo se formó la corteza de Marte y cómo el agua cambió la roca hace mucho tiempo. Su composición mineral coincide con partes de las tierras altas del sur de Marte vistas por los orbitadores de la NASA. Esta meteorita ofrece a los científicos una mirada rara a la superficie antigua de Marte y a la actividad del agua, ayudando a entender mejor el ambiente temprano del planeta.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores esperan estudiar más a Teghaza 001 y usar métodos similares en otras meteoritas marcianas o muestras espaciales. Esto podría revelar aún más sobre la historia de Marte y posiblemente de otros planetas.

**Frase clave** – Una meteorita marciana de 4.1 mil millones de años encontrada en la Tierra ofrece nuevas pistas sobre la corteza antigua del Planeta Rojo y su historia con el agua gracias a una datación mineral precisa.
